goal: Teach frontend-oriented AEM developers to keep HTL readable, markup-focused and context-safe while rendering configured and missing Guide Card data.

deck_context.source_summary: Class 11 of a seven-week AEM Sites course, delivered Monday, August 31, 2026. The audience understands Resources, Sling resolution, editable templates, policies, dialogs, persisted properties and accessible image delivery. This class begins Week 3 by connecting authored Guide Card data to safe, readable HTL and observable DOM states.
deck_context.core_claim: HTL should expose a small view contract: prepared values enter, semantic markup and deliberate states are rendered, and each expression is escaped for the context where its output lands.
canonical_facts: HTL is AEM's preferred server-side template language for HTML.
HTL expressions use ${...}; block statements use data-sly-* attributes.
HTL owns direct markup production while complex business logic belongs in Java such as a Sling Model or service.
data-sly-test conditionally keeps or removes an element.
data-sly-list repeats markup for a collection.
Use an existing semantic HTML element for block statements when possible; use sly only when no suitable element exists.
data-sly-template and data-sly-call reuse small markup fragments with explicit inputs.
HTL automatically applies context-aware escaping for HTML text, attributes and known URI attributes.
URI values such as href and src are validated and unsafe values can be removed.
Expressions inside JavaScript and CSS require explicit display contexts such as scriptString and styleString.
context='unsafe' disables XSS protection and must not be used as a shortcut.
The Guide Card review covers configured, empty-author and empty-visitor outcomes.

slides.title: Keep the template boundary narrow.
slides.intent: Separate data preparation from direct markup production.
key_points: HTL owns elements, attributes, conditions and iteration
Resource properties and model getters provide view values
Sling Models or services own complex preparation and business rules
Readable HTL makes the rendered contract easy to review
Extract logic only when the view would otherwise become hard to explain or repeat

slides.title: Expressions read values where the markup needs them.
slides.intent: Teach concise value access while keeping names aligned with the rendered HTML.
key_points: ${properties.title} reads the current Resource property
${card.title} reads a prepared getter exposed through data-sly-use
Text, ordinary attributes and URI attributes are different contexts
Meaningful identifiers make templates easier to review
A direct expression is clearer than a temporary variable with no purpose

slides.title: Templates and calls reuse small markup contracts.
slides.intent: Prevent repetition without creating a private component framework inside HTL.

data-sly-call invokes it with named values
Reuse one stable purpose with a small input contract
Keep component responsibility visible at the call site
Repeat simple markup when an abstraction would hide the output

slides.title: Output context is part of the security contract.
slides.intent: Show what HTL infers automatically and where an explicit display context is mandatory.
key_points: HTL automatically escapes HTML text and ordinary attributes
href and src use URI validation
JavaScript and CSS require explicit display contexts
context='html' filters allowed markup
Never use context='unsafe' as an escaping shortcut

slides.title: Key takeaways
slides.intent: Retrieve the five rules for maintainable HTL.
key_points: HTL renders the view; models and services prepare complex values
Direct expressions keep the source-to-markup relationship visible
Conditions and lists include a deliberate empty outcome
Templates reuse small markup contracts, not speculative frameworks
Output context matches where the value is rendered
